question: Why did 74% of streaming users think their playlists held no fully AI-generated music when nearly 57% of Deezer's October joiners already had at least one such track?

rungs.question: Why do the two figures point in opposite directions?
rungs.answer: They measure different things in different groups. The 74% is what surveyed streaming users believed about their own playlists. The 57% is what Deezer found in the imported playlists of more than 53,000 people who moved to Deezer from other services in October. Nobody was measured both ways.

evidence.quote: The 57% is drawn from Deezer’s internal data on new subscribers joining from other streaming platforms, not from the Ipsos survey sample.
This number is based on Deezer’s internal data on new subscribers joining from other streaming platforms, not specifically from those surveyed.
according to Deezer’s internal data a majority of new subscribers joining from other streaming platforms, had 100 % AI-generated music in their library.

counter.text: Deezer's chief executive presents the two figures as one gap between belief and reality: "there is a significant gap between what listeners think is in their playlists and what is actually there" (all three readable sources quote him). The sources do not show the two groups are alike.

rungs.question: Why does Deezer count those tracks as fully AI-generated?
rungs.answer: Deezer runs its own AI-detection tool and tags albums that hold fully AI tracks. The sources describe the tool, and Deezer says it can make false positives. None says outright that the 57% came from that tool, though it is the only detection method the sources name.

evidence.quote: Deezer added that it has tuned its AI-detection tool “to achieve maximum accuracy,” but that false positives may occur.

The Paris-based company also introduced the “world’s first AI tagging system for music streaming” last year, clearly displaying which albums include fully AI generated tracks, and also launched a free online AI music detector, covering multiple DSPs, this summer.

counter.text: Deezer itself says false positives may occur, so some share of the 57% may be human-made tracks flagged in error; no source gives an error rate. Searched: the three readable sources.

rungs.question: Why are so many fully AI tracks around to end up in playlists?
rungs.answer: The supply is very large. Deezer says it receives nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks a day, more than half of its daily deliveries on peak days, and that most streams of such tracks in 2025 were fraudulent. Only one readable source gives these figures.

evidence.quote: Deezer says it is receiving nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks every day, accounting for more than 50% of its total daily deliveries on peak days.
Deezer says up to 85% of the streams generated by fully AI-generated tracks in 2025 were fraudulent, and that it excludes manipulated streams from royalty payments.

counter.text: These are Deezer's figures for tracks delivered to Deezer; the 57% concerns playlists built on other services, and no source gives delivery figures for those services. Searched: the three readable sources.

rungs.question: Why would listeners not notice those tracks in their own playlists?
rungs.answer: The sources point to two reasons without stating them as the cause: most people cannot tell fully AI music from human music by ear, and labelling is not yet standard on streaming services, which is why the RIAA and IFPI are pushing for tags.

evidence.quote: The first edition of the study, published in November 2025, found that 97% of respondents couldn’t tell fully AI-generated music apart from human-made music in a blind test.
The findings come as the RIAA and IFPI lead a push for streaming services to label AI-made tracks.
They want the content identified. They want the content labeled.

counter.text: None found on what the other services, where these playlists were built, actually show listeners; the readable sources do not describe their labelling. Searched: the three readable sources.

landing.shows: The headline gap sets a belief measured in a survey of streaming users against a count Deezer made with its own detector on a different group, people who moved their playlists to Deezer from other services. The sources point to a huge supply of AI tracks, ears that cannot tell them apart and little labelling elsewhere, but they stop before saying what the other services show listeners.
landing.open_question: If most listeners cannot hear the difference and their service never labels it, what would it take for anyone to know what is in their own playlist?
